heading: Do induction heads explain most loss improvement across token positions in large transformers?
definition: induction heads are the mechanism behind most in-context learning (loss falling with token index) in large transformers, not just small ones.
summary: Independent studies support a causal role for induction heads in reducing loss on later tokens relative to earlier tokens. Whether they explain most of this improvement in large transformers remains an open question.

suggested_status.by_scale: toy: R0 for the original small attention-only baseline (arXiv:2209.11895#R6), without an independent verdict on the original. <1B: ?; below 160M, exclusion ablation of induction heads (those with low FV scores) has no significant token-loss-difference effect beyond random ablation (arXiv:2502.14010#R5), a condition-specific null in pretrained models rather than a failed replication of the original's attention-only setting; causal involvement is supported in the aggregate over 345M, without a measured majority share (arXiv:2502.14010#R7). The 2-layer GPT2 prefix-matching-penalty result (arXiv:2502.18802#r9, arXiv:2502.18802#r10) has no V3 verdict. 1-10B: ?; independent support for induction-related all-sample token-loss gains at 1B (arXiv:2511.05743#R10, arXiv:2511.05743#R11, arXiv:2511.05743#R12), with non-extractive token-loss difference retained under HAPAX but described as statistically indifferent (arXiv:2511.05743#R14); the main 1B comparisons use one seed per condition, and this study's source check was a partial read. 10-100B: ? for V3 as written; counts: versions.V3.studies_by_size includes this bucket, but classification-accuracy results do not establish a majority contribution to token-index loss, and the cited loss-ablation rows are aggregated rather than bucket-specific. >100B: ?; counts: versions.V3.studies_by_size has no >100B key.
suggested_status.reason: ? because the rules' definition of C is not met, and the records do not yet support any other level. C requires a failed replication or a credible artifact argument. The two condition-specific results the earlier C rested on (arXiv:2502.14010#R5, arXiv:2511.05743#R14) are neither, and no study measures the majority share. In models over 345M, exclusion ablation of induction heads affects token-loss difference more than exclusion ablation of function-vector heads (arXiv:2502.14010#R7). This comparative effect persists at the largest scales despite a shrinking gap; that gap does not establish a declining induction-mediated share (arXiv:2502.14010#R8). Below 160M, the exclusion intervention has no significant effect beyond random ablation (arXiv:2502.14010#R5). That null comes from pretrained models under exclusion ablation, and the verdict calls the size cutoff ambiguous. The original's ICL-score drop comes from small attention-only models under pattern-preserving ablation (arXiv:2209.11895#R6). In GPT-NeoX-based 1B models, targeted training-loss masking removes the all-sample token-loss-difference gain, supporting induction-related copying as a contributor to that metric (arXiv:2511.05743#R10, arXiv:2511.05743#R11, arXiv:2511.05743#R12). On non-extractive samples, HAPAX retains token-loss difference with weak induction heads; the text describes it as higher while also statistically indifferent (arXiv:2511.05743#R14). The main 1B comparisons use a single seed per condition. The source check of this study was a partial read that could not verify Figure 7's numbers, so R14 is not yet confirmed against the full text. Few-shot retention at 1B and 2.8B instead bears on V6. Qwen2.5-3B induction-head ablation severely impairs synthetic repetitive-sequence prediction relative to random controls; residual above-chance accuracy is supportive of a major task-specific role, rather than evidence of a shrinking share (arXiv:2509.21534#r13, arXiv:2509.21534#r16). These task results do not estimate the share of broad token-index-loss improvement. ICL-score interventions sit in a fits-no-version theme with closest version V3 and have no V3 verdict. Penalising prefix-matching attention while training 2-layer GPT2 keeps PS near zero and lowers the ICL score (arXiv:2502.18802#r9, arXiv:2502.18802#r10). Ablating the top 10% CMR-like heads worsens the C4 ICL score (500th minus 50th token loss) more than random ablation in most models, with several comparisons n.s. (arXiv:2405.14992#R13, arXiv:2405.14992#R14, arXiv:2405.14992#R15). Those heads are chosen as CMR-like by CMR distance, not by induction score, and the packs give only a finding summary for these rows (arXiv:2405.14992#f2), without per-model sizes. The same theme lists arXiv:2509.22947#R37, arXiv:2509.22947#R38, arXiv:2509.22947#R39, arXiv:2509.22947#R40, arXiv:2509.22947#R41 and arXiv:2509.22947#R42 (e.g. −22.6% natural-only vs −4.9% Induction curriculum at 0.13B, arXiv:2509.22947#f1). However, the study's V6 verdict reason describes that ablation measure as 10-shot function-probe accuracy, not token-index loss. Counts: versions.V3.verdicts.supports.studies = 7, versions.V3.verdicts.limits_scope.studies = 8, and versions.V3.verdicts.challenges.studies = 2 are the supplied pre-correction totals; they do not incorporate the checker's label changes. Counts: versions.V3.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 0 supports treating the retained tests as independent of the original author group. The author lists also show no shared authors with an original for arXiv:2502.18802, arXiv:2405.14992 or arXiv:2509.22947.
suggested_status.open_questions: Three steps would let a level be set from these records. (1) Iris sets one rule, applied to all seven versions, for whether a condition-specific challenge gives C or R2 with a stated scope limit. (2) A full re-read of arXiv:2511.05743 covers R14's 'higher' versus 'statistically indifferent' wording, Figure 7 and the seed details. (3) Iris confirms that V3 means token-index loss only. If so, V3 verdicts are run on arXiv:2502.18802#r9, arXiv:2502.18802#r10, arXiv:2405.14992#R13, arXiv:2405.14992#R14 and arXiv:2405.14992#R15, with the per-model sizes behind the arXiv:2405.14992 rows. arXiv:2509.22947's ablation rows (R37-R42) need a V3 verdict only if their measure turns out to be token-index loss; its V6 verdict reason describes 10-shot function-probe accuracy. If V3 also covers classification accuracy, arXiv:2505.18752, arXiv:2407.07011, arXiv:2509.24164 and arXiv:2601.20796 return as tests. arXiv:2505.18752 and arXiv:2509.24164 share authors (Hao-Lin Yang, Hakaze Cho, Naoya Inoue), so they count as one group. Beyond these records: measure the share of token-index-loss improvement removed by induction-head interventions in large transformers, with size- and layer-matched random controls. Report all-sample and non-extractive results separately to test the distinction in arXiv:2511.05743#R10 and arXiv:2511.05743#R14. Resolve the scale dependence of exclusion ablation reported in arXiv:2502.14010#R5 and arXiv:2502.14010#R7 with bucket-specific loss results, especially at 10-100B. A reproducible majority contribution across these conditions would support R2 for the full claim; reproducibly small contributions would support C. Test above 100B, absent from counts: versions.V3.studies_by_size.

source.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
source.authors: Catherine Olsson; Nelson Elhage; Neel Nanda; Nicholas Joseph; Nova DasSarma; T. Henighan; Benjamin Mann; Amanda Askell; Yuntao Bai; Anna Chen; Tom Conerly; Dawn Drain; Deep Ganguli; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; Danny Hernandez; Scott Johnston; Andy Jones; John Kernion; Liane Lovitt; Kamal Ndousse; D. original_result.setup: The authors ablated (disabled) individual attention heads in small models both with MLPs (feedforward layers) and without them.
original_result.result: The original study attributed almost all in-context learning—learning from the current context—in small attention-only models to induction heads. In models with MLPs (feedforward layers), the evidence was suggestive but not conclusive.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: Removing induction-predictable training signal eliminated all-sample token-loss-difference gains at 1B.
Induction-head ablation reduced repetitive-sequence prediction to chance in Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B.
Induction-head interventions removed at least 90% of in-context learning benefits in selected classification settings.
Ablating top induction heads collapsed classification accuracy across seven models from 2B to 70B.
Above 345M parameters, induction-head ablation reduced loss drops with position more than ablating task-encoding function-vector heads.
Training interventions linked induction-head formation to loss dropping later in text in small Pythia models.
Removing heads attending to the previous token stopped context-driven gains when tracing grid paths in Llama-3.1-8B.
Thresholded-HAPAX reduced abstractive accuracy at 1B, with heavy masking complicating interpretation.
Ablating heads attending to labels mainly disrupted recognition of valid labels across six models.
Qwen2.5-3B retained above-chance sequence prediction after severe impairment from induction-head ablation.
Induction-head interventions left residual classification benefits, with removal varying by model and ablation fraction.
Random-head ablation also reduced classification accuracy, weakening evidence that the damage was specific to induction heads.
Induction heads’ extra effect on loss drops later in text narrowed as model size increased.
Ablating induction heads removed about two-thirds of Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct’s accuracy advantage over chance.
Accuracy at tracing grid paths kept improving with more context after induction-head ablation in Llama-3.1-8B.
Non-extractive token-loss difference improved despite few, weak induction heads at 1B.
Below 160M parameters, induction-head ablation’s effect on token loss did not significantly exceed random-head ablation’s.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

untested.what: Loss falling with token index on natural text in models of 10B or more, under any intervention. Every >=10B test in this pack measures few-shot or classification accuracy.
untested.basis: The untested-parts lines of arXiv:2407.07011, arXiv:2505.18752 and arXiv:2509.24164 say loss by token index is not measured. Token-loss rows come only from arXiv:2502.14010 (aggregate over 345M), arXiv:2511.05743 (1B) and arXiv:2601.21996 (small Pythia). counts: V3.coverage_by_operation.measurement.by_size has only 1-10B; V3.coverage_by_operation.removal.by_size 10-100B: 3 are accuracy studies.

untested.what: The share of all in-context learning that induction heads carry ('most'). No study estimates a fraction of total ICL; the shares reported are of one task's ICL benefit, or are comparisons with FV or random ablation.
untested.basis: Untested-parts lines: arXiv:2407.07011 ('No share of all ICL is estimated'), arXiv:2505.18752, arXiv:2509.24164, arXiv:2502.14010 (compared with FV and random ablation, not total ICL), arXiv:2601.21996, lw:qtdSzLpQ8BXv6YANd. The original's untested line says the large-model majority claim rests on correlation and analogy.
counts: V3.studies_by_size has keys 1-10B: 7, 10-100B: 3, not stated: 2, <1B: 2 and no >100B key. The largest models in the pack are the 70B models of arXiv:2505.18752.

untested.what: Training-time removal of the induction signal above 2.8B. In other words, whether abstractive ICL survives without induction heads at large scale.
untested.basis: The untested line of arXiv:2511.05743 says models above 2.8B are not tested. counts: V3.coverage_by_operation.training.by_size has 1-10B: 1 and not stated: 1.

untested.what: Generation or other non-classification ICL in models of 10B or more under induction-head ablation.
untested.basis: arXiv:2505.18752's problems line calls its generation-task analysis preliminary. The untested line of arXiv:2509.24164 lists non-classification ICL. The non-classification tasks in the pack (arXiv:2509.21534 synthetic sequences, lw:qtdSzLpQ8BXv6YANd grid tracing, arXiv:2511.05743 abstractive tasks) are at or below 8B.

wording_issues.issue: The cited classification studies measure task accuracy rather than token-index loss; those results do not directly test V3. arXiv:2511.05743 reports that all-sample token-loss difference is dominated by copying (R10–R12). At 1B, HAPAX has higher non-extractive token-loss difference despite far fewer induction heads, but the text also describes the comparison as statistically indifferent (R14). This challenges dependence on strong induction heads for non-extractive token-loss improvement, without establishing a statistically significant improvement.

The cited task-specific reductions do not measure the share of token-index-loss improvement attributable to induction heads. In arXiv:2407.07011, Llama-3-8B ten-shot Repetition accuracy falls from 91.3% to 59.7% with 1% mean-ablation (R04), and to 51.5% with 3% mean-ablation (R06). In arXiv:2601.20796, Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct induction-head knockout on Open-MI reduces accuracy from 0.74 to 0.58 against 0.50 chance, removing about two-thirds of above-chance accuracy (r16). These classification results cannot determine V3 as written; residual performance alone does not contradict 'most'.

The cited mechanistic comparisons concern task accuracy, leaving their relevance to V3's token-index-loss mechanism undetermined. arXiv:2509.24164 attributes the accuracy loss from induction-head ablation mainly to predictions leaving the label set, a task-recognition effect (r3, r4). arXiv:2511.05743 finds function-vector heads causally more important than prefix-matching heads for abstractive task accuracy (R22), evidence relevant to V6. In arXiv:2505.18752's Llama2-70B label-absent condition, previous-token-head ablation hurts classification accuracy more than induction-head ablation (r22, r23); this comparison should not be generalized across models or treated as a direct V3 test.

The cited tests identify heads through operational proxies: prefix-matching score in arXiv:2407.07011, label-token attention in arXiv:2509.24164 (r3), and attention patterns in lw:qtdSzLpQ8BXv6YANd. In the lw study's copying-sufficient task, previous-token-head ablation produces a plateau (r4), while induction-head ablation leaves improvement intact (r1, r2). This does not measure token-index loss. In arXiv:2601.20796's Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct Open-MI task, accuracy falls from 0.74 to 0.65 after previous-token-head knockout, to 0.58 after induction-head knockout, and to 0.56 after combined knockout (r15–r17). Induction-head knockout has the larger individual effect; combined knockout cannot be attributed to previous-token heads alone. These accuracy results do not determine V3.

wording_issues.phrase: in large transformers, not just small ones
wording_issues.issue: Classification-accuracy results reach 70B in arXiv:2505.18752 (r01), Qwen2.5-32B and Yi-34B in arXiv:2509.24164 (r18, r20), but do not establish V3's token-index-loss mechanism at those sizes. counts: versions.V3.studies_by_size has no >100B entry. The small-model premise comes from the original's small attention-only models (arXiv:2209.11895 R6). In small pretrained models below 160M, exclusion ablation has no significant token-loss effect (arXiv:2502.14010 R5).

method_sensitivity.what: arXiv:2502.14010 reports that the relative effects of induction-head and function-vector (FV) ablation differ between few-shot accuracy and token-loss difference. arXiv:2511.05743 at 1B: all-sample token-loss difference appears to worsen under HAPAX training (R11), while non-extractive token-loss difference is reported as higher than Vanilla but statistically indifferent (R14). Thus the predicted dependence on strong induction heads is absent for the non-extractive measure. The few-shot accuracy comparison belongs to V6.

lw:qtdSzLpQ8BXv6YANd: in Llama-3.1-8B grid tracing, induction-head ablation lowers accuracy but improvement with context continues (r1, r2), while top-32 previous-token-head ablation makes accuracy plateau (r4). This comparison concerns context-driven task performance; token-index loss and the share of all ICL are unmeasured.

arXiv:2502.14010: under exclusion ablation in pretrained models, induction-head ablation has no significant token-loss-difference effect beyond random below 160M (R5). Over 345M, its effect exceeds FV ablation (R7); this comparison persists at the largest scales while the gap shrinks (R8). arXiv:2509.21534: zeroing all identified induction heads reduces prediction accuracy on synthetic repetitive second- and third-order hierarchical sequences to chance in Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B (r11, r12), and severely reduces it while leaving it above chance in Qwen2.5-3B (r13); the 3B random-head control has small or negligible effects (r16). Neither the shrinking comparative gap nor residual above-chance accuracy establishes a declining induction-head share of total ICL.

Head sets are chosen differently across studies. arXiv:2502.14010 uses exclusion ablation: induction-head ablation preserves the top 2% FV-scoring heads by excluding them from its targets; FV ablation similarly preserves the top 2% induction-scoring heads. Its method line reports sensitivity to this selection. arXiv:2509.24164 identifies heads by attention to label tokens at a top-3% threshold and also examines other thresholds. The latter concerns classification-task mechanisms; token-index loss and the share of all ICL remain unmeasured.

status_amendment.public_note: This version's level changed from C to ?, meaning it cannot yet be decided: the two results behind the earlier C hold only under particular conditions and are neither a failed replication nor evidence that the effect is an artifact. One of them still has to be checked against the full paper, and some experiments that measure loss by token position have not yet been assessed for this version.
status_amendment.level_changed_because: C to ?. The rules define C as a failed replication or a credible artifact argument. V3's C rested on two condition-specific results, and neither meets that definition. arXiv:2502.14010#R5 is a null for exclusion ablation of induction heads in pretrained models below 160M, which is not the original's attention-only setting, and the same study supports causal involvement over 345M. arXiv:2511.05743#R14 is a comparison the source calls statistically indifferent, and the source check of that study was a partial read, not yet redone in full. In addition, token-index ICL-score interventions from arXiv:2502.18802 and arXiv:2405.14992 have never had V3 verdicts. R2 is not assigned either, because no independent study measures the majority share. The level cannot be told from these records until Iris sets the rule for condition-specific challenges, arXiv:2511.05743 is re-read, and those verdicts are run.
